assessment.rationale: The spans state that Spain ceded Louisiana to France in 1800 via the Third Treaty of San Ildefonso, and that France then sold it to the United States in 1803. Thus, Spain did not cede Louisiana directly to the United States.

excerpts.text: The [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_France "Early modern France") had controlled the Louisiana territory from 1682[[4]](#cite_note-6) until [it was ceded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_(New_Spain) "Louisiana (New Spain)") to [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") in 1762.

Throughout the second half of the 18th century, the French colony of Louisiana became a pawn for European political intrigue.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHerring200899-8) The colony was the most substantial presence of [France's overseas empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire "French colonial empire"), though its population was sparse and largely concentrated in small settlements along the Mississippi River and its tributaries. France ceded the territory to Spain in 1762 in the secret [Treaty of Fontainebleau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fontainebleau_(1762) "Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762)"). Following French defeat in the [Seven Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Years'_War "Seven Years' War"), Spain gained control of the [territory west of the Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_(New_Spain) "Louisiana (New Spain)"), and the British received the territory to the east of the river.[[*[[Wikipedia:Citing\_sources|page needed]]*]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeinig1995[[Category:Wikipedia_articles_needing_page_number_citations_from_February_2015]]<sup_class=)-9">[7]

However, in 1800, Spain had ceded the Louisiana territory back to France as part of Napoleon's secret [Third Treaty of San Ildefonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Treaty_of_San_Ildefonso "Third Treaty of San Ildefonso").[[8]](#cite_note-10) The subsequent 1801 [Treaty of Aranjuez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Aranjuez_(1801) "Treaty of Aranjuez (1801)") established that Spain's cession of Louisiana was a "restoration" of the territory to France, not a retrocession.[[9]](#cite_note-Chambers-11) The territory nominally remained under Spanish control, until a transfer of power to France on November 30, 1803, just three weeks before the formal cession of the territory to the United States on December 20, 1803.[[10]](#cite_note-12)

excerpts.text:
"His Catholic Majesty promises and engages on his part to cede to the French Republic six months after the full and entire execution of the conditions and Stipulations herein relative to his Royal Highness the Duke of Parma, the Colony or Province of Louisiana with the Same extent that it now has in the hand of Spain, & that it had when France possessed it; and Such as it Should be after the Treaties subsequently entered into between Spain and other States."

And whereas in pursuance of the Treaty and particularly of the third article the French Republic has an incontestible title to the domain and to the possession of the said Territory--The First Consul of the French Republic desiring to give to the United States a strong proof of his friendship doth hereby cede to the United States in the name of the French Republic for ever and in full Sovereignty the said territory with all its rights and appurtenances as fully and in the Same manner as they have been acquired by the French Republic in virtue of the above mentioned Treaty concluded with his Catholic Majesty.

The President of the United States of America and the First Consul of the French Republic in the name of the French people, in consequence of the treaty of cession of Louisiana which has been Signed this day; wishing to regulate definitively every thing which has relation to the Said cession have authorized to this effect the Plenipotentiaries, that is to say the President of the United States has, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate of the Said States, nominated for their Plenipoten tiaries, Robert R. Livingston, Minister Plenipotentiary of the United States, and James Monroe, Minister Plenipotentiary and Envoy-Extraordinary of the Said United States, near the Government of the French Republic; and the First Consul of the French Republic, in the name of the French people, has named as Pleniopotentiary of the Said Republic the citizen Francis Barbé Marbois: who, in virtue of their full powers, which have been exchanged this day, have agreed to the followings articles:
